idiom_name: identity-key column plus mapper resolve/write step (optional identity map)
implementation_notes: Every single-valued association becomes one column on the referencing side holding the referenced object's identity key; the domain class keeps a real object reference and never sees the key. On save the mapper asks the referenced object for its identity field and writes that value into the column (after the referenced row exists); on load it reads the key and resolves it to an object, either immediately, on first access (lazy) or through a per-session identity map that guarantees one object per row. Collections cannot live in a column: a one-to-many moves the key to the many side and a many-to-many needs an association table, and the write order must follow the dependency (referenced object first) unless the constraint is deferrable.
code_sketch:
# rows: orders(id, customer_id) -> customers(id)
customer = identity_map.get(order.customer_id) or customers.find(order.customer_id)
order.customer = customer            # in-memory reference restored from the key
# save, parent first:
customers.upsert(customer)
orders.update(order.id, customer_id=customer.id)
pitfalls: Resolving the key only sometimes: once raw key values appear in the domain layer the object graph has silently become a relational access layer.
Writing the referencing row before the referenced row exists violates the constraint (or, without one, leaves an orphan key that only fails later).
No identity map means two loads of the same referenced row produce two objects, so in-memory identity no longer matches database identity.
Setting FetchType.EAGER on @ManyToOne/@OneToOne (JPA default) without a fetch plan produces N+1 on every list query; EAGER cannot be overridden per-query (HHH-8776).
Treating optional @OneToOne as LAZY when the FK is nullable — Hibernate ignores LAZY on optional to-one associations unless optional=false, silently loading the proxy immediately.
Relying on ORM cascade delete (orphanRemoval, DeleteBehavior.Cascade) without a corresponding ON DELETE rule in the database schema, leading to orphaned child rows on bulk deletes.
Combining soft-delete entities with database-level ON DELETE CASCADE — the DB cascade fires on hard delete, silently deleting children that the application expects to be retained.
Using composite natural keys as FK targets and failing to map all key columns correctly; equals()/hashCode() on the composite id type becomes mandatory.
Bidirectional parent-child with insertable=false,updatable=false on the inverse side: forgetting to set the owning side leaves the FK null at flush, silently orphaning the child.
Cyclical references without post_update (SQLAlchemy), flush ordering (Hibernate InsertActionSorter), or deferred constraints (PostgreSQL/SQLite): the first insert fails with a constraint violation.

Wrong move: declaring the association only in the ORM (Rails belongs_to without foreign_key: true, a relationship with no constraint in the migration) -> the database accepts orphan keys the moment any script, report or service writes SQL directly -> instead add the real DB-level foreign key constraint in the migration and treat the ORM association as navigation sugar over it.

Wrong move: running an FK-less emulation mode (Prisma relationMode=prisma) on tables other writers touch -> the emulation only guards writes routed through that client, so concurrent writers leave dangling relation fields -> instead keep relationMode=foreignKeys so the database enforces the rule, or make the ORM the sole writer.

Wrong move: hand-writing SQL against the object field name -> Django and Rails both store the key in a <field>_id column (author, not author_id / author), so raw queries, views and triggers break with unknown-column errors -> instead use the framework's column convention or set db_column / foreign_key: / @map explicitly and verify against the actual schema.
